paragraphs: To find the rules of society that suit nations best, we would need a superior intelligence that could see all of men’s passions without feeling any of them. It would have to have no kinship with our nature, yet know it thoroughly. Its happiness would have to be independent of ours, and yet it would have to be willing to care about ours. And finally, it would have to look ahead to a distant glory as time goes by, working in one century and able to enjoy the result in another.[1] It would take gods to give men laws.

Caligula argued from the facts what Plato, in his dialogue the _Politicus_, argued from right when he defined the civil or kingly man. But if great princes are rare, great legislators are far rarer. A prince has only to follow the pattern a legislator must lay down. The legislator is the engineer who invents the machine; the prince is merely the mechanic who assembles it and keeps it running. “At the birth of societies,” says Montesquieu, “the leaders of Republics create the institutions, and afterward the institutions form the leaders.”[2]

Anyone who dares to set up the institutions of a people must feel able, so to speak, to change human nature. He must be able to turn each individual, who is by himself a complete and solitary whole, into a part of a larger whole from which that individual in some way receives his life and being. He must be able to alter man’s constitution in order to strengthen it, and to put a partial, moral existence in place of the physical and independent existence that nature gave us all. In a word, he must take away man’s own resources and give him new ones that are foreign to him and that he cannot use without the help of others. The more completely these natural resources are destroyed, the greater and more lasting are the ones he acquires, and the more solid and perfect the institutions. So when each citizen is nothing and can do nothing without all the others, and the resources acquired by the whole equal or exceed the sum of all the individuals’ resources, we may say that legislation has reached the highest point of perfection it can.

In every respect the legislator holds an extraordinary position in the State. He holds it through his genius, and just as much through his office, which is neither magistracy nor Sovereignty. This office, which establishes the Republic, has no place anywhere in its constitution. It is a singular, superior function with nothing in common with human rule. For if the one who commands men should not command the laws, then the one who commands the laws should not command men either. Otherwise his laws would be servants of his passions and would often only perpetuate his injustices, and his private aims would inevitably spoil the sanctity of his work.

When Lycurgus gave laws to his country, he began by giving up the throne. Most Greek towns customarily left the drafting of their laws to foreigners. The Republics of modern Italy often followed this example, and Geneva did too, to its benefit.[3] At the height of its prosperity, Rome saw every crime of tyranny come back to life and came close to destruction, because it put legislative authority and sovereign power in the same hands.

Yet the decemvirs themselves never claimed the right to pass any law on their own authority alone. “Nothing we propose to you,” they told the people, “can become law without your consent. Romans, make yourselves the authors of the laws that are to bring you happiness.”

So the person who drafts the laws has no right to legislate, or should have none. And the people cannot give up this right even if they want to, because it cannot be passed to anyone else: under the fundamental compact only the general will binds individuals, and there is no way to be sure that a particular will agrees with the general will until it has been put to the free vote of the people. I have said this before, but it is worth repeating.
So the work of legislation brings together two things that seem incompatible: an undertaking beyond human powers, and, to carry it out, an authority that is no authority.

There is a further difficulty worth noting. Wise men who try to address the common herd in their own language rather than the herd’s cannot possibly be understood. There are a thousand kinds of ideas that cannot be put into popular language. Ideas that are too general and objects that are too remote are equally out of its reach. Each individual cares only for the plan of government that serves his own interest, and finds it hard to see the benefits he might draw from the constant sacrifices that good laws demand. For a young people to appreciate sound principles of political theory and follow the basic rules of statecraft, the effect would have to become the cause. The social spirit, which the institutions are meant to create, would have to guide their very founding, and men would have to be, before the law, what the law is to make them. The legislator therefore cannot appeal to force or to reason, and must turn to an authority of a different kind, one that can compel without violence and persuade without convincing.

This is what has always driven the founders of nations to appeal to divine intervention and to credit the gods with their own wisdom. They did so in order that peoples, obeying the laws of the State as they obey the laws of nature, and recognizing the same power in the making of the city as in the making of man, might obey freely and bear the yoke of the public happiness submissively.

This sublime reason, far beyond the reach of the common herd, is the reason whose decisions the legislator puts in the mouths of the immortals, in order to compel by divine authority those whom human prudence could not move.[4] But not everyone can make the gods speak, or be believed when he declares himself their interpreter. The great soul of the legislator is the one miracle that can prove his mission. Any man can carve stone tablets, buy an oracle, claim secret communion with some god, train a bird to whisper in his ear, or find other crude ways to deceive the people. Someone whose knowledge goes no further may gather a band of fools, but he will never found an empire, and his extravagances will soon die with him. Idle tricks create only a passing bond; only wisdom can make one last. The Judaic law, which still survives, and the law of the child of Ishmael, which has ruled half the world for ten centuries, still proclaim the great men who laid them down. And while the pride of philosophy and the blind spirit of faction see in them nothing but lucky impostures, the true political theorist admires in the institutions they founded the great and powerful genius that presides over things built to last.

From this we should not conclude, as Warburton does, that politics and religion share a common object among us. The conclusion is rather that in the earliest periods of nations, one is used as an instrument of the other.
